A primary school tells me 'we're just not getting enough new pupils.' How do we help them?

Their complaint is low enrollment. The real problem is almost never 'not enough adverts' — it's two missing systems: a clear story, and a follow-up that doesn't drop. Most schools get inquiries on WhatsApp and lose half of them because no one replies fast or tracks who visited.

Highest-leverage fix: a simple enrollment pipeline. Every inquiry logged, a same-day warm reply, an info pack, a booked visit, a reminder. That alone usually lifts conversion more than any billboard.

Tier: start them on Catalyst — it gives them visibility and the enrollment queue. 30-day win: "every parent who asks about your school gets a reply within an hour and a booked visit." Next step: ask for their current term's inquiry numbers so we can show them how many they're leaking.

How should a small Ugandan school market for next term's intake?

Forget billboards first — your best marketing is the parents you already have. Three moves, in order:

1. Turn current parents into your sales team. One WhatsApp broadcast: "Intake for next term is open — if you know a family looking for a good school, send them our way." Warm referrals convert better than any ad here.
2. Show, don't tell. Three short phone-shot videos — a normal class, a happy teacher, a parent saying why they chose you. Post to your status and the school group. Story beats slogans.
3. Close fast. Whoever inquires, reply same day, book a visit. Speed is the whole game.

Next step: pick the 20 most active parents in your WhatsApp list — that's your first referral push this week.

A school has 180 students and tracks fees on paper in a book. Which NEXT tier, and why?

Builder. Here's the math, not the pitch: at 180 students a bursar burns roughly 12 hours a week chasing and reconciling fees by hand. That's about 50 hours a month. Builder gives them the fee ledger, automated reminders, and Nia watching collection daily — the system pays for itself inside the first two weeks of saved time, before you even count the fees it recovers.

Catalyst would feel cheap but leave them still doing manual reconciliation. Don't undersell them into frustration. Next step: get one screenshot of their fee book — I'll turn it into a one-page 'before/after' you can show the head teacher.

A church says they need 'help with their image and also managing their members.' Is that Charis or NEXT?

Both — and that's the strongest kind of client. 'Image' is Charis: their story, their media, how they show up. 'Managing members' is NEXT: a Church OS for membership, giving, and communication.

Lead with Charis (the story), because once the story is clear the systems gap becomes obvious and the NEXT conversation sells itself. Next step: book one meeting, bring both hats, but open with their story — ask them "what do you want people to feel about this church?"

A head teacher says $149 a month is too expensive. What do I say?

Don't defend the price — reframe it against what they already spend. "A part-time bursar costs you about UGX 600,000 a month. Catalyst is less than that, it works 24/7, it never asks for tea, and it doesn't forget to send the fee reminder. You're not adding a cost — you're replacing hours of admin with a system that pays for itself the first time it recovers one overdue term's fees."

Then go quiet and let them do the math. Next step: offer the first-3-schools deal — implementation fee waived for a video testimonial.

An NGO says donor reporting takes them forever every quarter. How do we advise them?

Their pain is the report. The real problem is that their data lives in five places — a spreadsheet, some photos, a WhatsApp group, someone's head — so every report is a fresh archaeology dig.

The fix isn't a better template, it's a single source of truth: beneficiaries, activities, and outcomes captured once, as they happen. Then the quarterly report is a button, not a week. That's an NGO OS on Builder.

The story angle is the multiplier: Charis turns those same outcomes into a donor film that raises the next round. Next step: ask them how many hours last quarter's report took — that hour count is your whole pitch.

"Six weeks ago, Peak Primary collected 71% of their term fees. The bursar chased the rest by hand, one parent at a time.

We wired NEXT OS in. Nia now spots every overdue account the morning it crosses the line and drafts a warm reminder for the head teacher to approve. No nagging. No spreadsheets.

Collection is climbing — and the bursar got her evenings back.

This is what Africa's intelligent future looks like. Not someday. This term."

Keep the numbers honest as they move. Next step: get one real line from the bursar to quote — a human voice beats any stat.

Don't sell her the feature, sell her the Friday. "Right now, every overdue account is a phone call you have to remember to make, on top of everything else. The bursar is the one who decides if this tool lives or dies. Win her, not just the head teacher. Next step: in the demo, let her tap 'approve' on a real draft — the feeling sells it.

How is NEXT different from just buying school management software?

School software is a filing cabinet — it stores what you put in and waits. NEXT is a chief of staff — it watches what's inside and tells you what matters before you ask. Software makes you log in to find the problem. Nia messages you the morning the problem starts.

And we don't hand you a login and leave. We build it around your school, train your people, and supervise it. You're not buying a tool, you're gaining a team member who never sleeps. Next step: show them the morning brief — that's the moment the difference clicks.

A client is hesitating. Should we just cut our price to close them?

Be careful — a price you drop to win is a price you can never raise, and a client who only signs on a discount churns the moment someone cheaper appears. Don't cut the price; change the shape. Offer the first-3-schools deal: waive the one-time setup fee in exchange for a video testimonial. They feel a win, you keep your price intact, and you walk away with a case study worth more than the discount.

Next step: name the testimonial as the trade out loud — "I'll waive setup if you'll let us film your story once it's working."

If a school can only automate one thing first, what should it be?

Fees. Always start where the money leaks. Attendance and reports matter, but fee collection is the bloodstream — fix that and the school can afford everything else, and the head teacher sees the value in the bank, not in a dashboard.

Visibility first (see every overdue account), then automation (reminders write themselves). Next step: ask for their current collection rate — the gap to 85% is the money sitting on the table, and that number opens the deal.

How should a school sound in its WhatsApp broadcasts to parents?

Like a trusted neighbour, not a notice board. Open by acknowledging the parent, keep it short, one message one purpose, and sign off with warmth — a Luganda phrase when it fits. Never send a wall of text or a cold 'Dear Parent.' Use first names where you can.

The test: would a busy mother feel respected reading this at a taxi stage on her phone? If yes, send it. Next step: set three reusable templates — fee reminder, attendance check, event notice — all in that voice, so staff stop writing cold ones.

What should NEXT actually deliver in a quarterly review with a school's leadership?

Three things, in their language, not ours: what changed (collection up X%, hours saved), what Nia caught that they'd have missed, and the one move for next quarter. Leadership doesn't want a feature list — they want proof their investment returned more than it cost, and a clear next step.

End every review with a single recommendation, not five. Next step: build a one-page board summary template so these reviews take an hour to prep, not a day.

An NGO wants to grow donations but has a tiny budget. What's the highest-leverage advice?

Stop asking for money and start showing outcomes. Donors give to proof, not pleas. With a small budget, your leverage is one well-told story a month — a single beneficiary, filmed honestly on a phone, with a real before and after. That's Charis territory, and it out-raises a glossy brochure every time.

Then make giving frictionless: mobile money link in every post. Next step: pick one beneficiary whose story is true and specific — specificity is what loosens wallets.

"You know how a good head teacher keeps the whole school in their head — who's behind on fees, which child stopped coming, which parent to call?
